## Problem 1
```{r,message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1)

birthday_repeated = function(n_room) {
  
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n_room, replace = TRUE)
  
  repeated_birthdays = length(unique(birthdays)) < n_room
  
  return(repeated_birthdays)
  
}

sim_results = 
  tibble(group_size = 2:50) |> 
  mutate(
    prob_repeated = map_dbl(
      group_size,
      \(n) mean(replicate(10000, birthday_repeated(n)))
    )
  )

sim_results |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = prob_repeated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of a shared birthday by group size",
    x = "Group size",
    y = "Probability of at least two shared birthdays"
  )
```
The probability of a shared birthday rises in an S-shaped curve with group size. It crosses 50% at about 23 people and reaches roughly 97% by 50. This is surprising because the number of pairs grows much faster than the number of people.

## Problem 2
```{r,message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
file_names = tibble(
  file = list.files("data", full.names = TRUE)
)

file_names = file_names %>%
  mutate(
    data = map(file, read_csv),
    file_name = basename(file),
    arm = if_else(
      str_detect(file_name, "^con"),
      "control",
      "experimental"
    ),
    subject_id = str_extract(file_name, "\\d+")
  )

longitudinal_df =
  file_names %>%
  unnest(data) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    week = as.integer(str_remove(week, "week_"))
  ) %>%
  select(subject_id, arm, week, observation)

# Create a spaghetti plot
ggplot(
  longitudinal_df,
  aes(
    x = week,
    y = observation,
    group = interaction(subject_id, arm),
    color = arm
  )
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Spaghetti Plot of Individual Outcomes Over Time",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Study Arm"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

longitudinal_df %>%
  distinct(subject_id, arm) %>%
  count(arm)

longitudinal_df %>%
  count(subject_id, arm)

longitudinal_df %>%
  summarize(
    missing = sum(is.na(observation))
  )
```

At week 1 the two arms are similar. Over 8 weeks the control arm stays roughly flat, while the experimental arm tends to increase. In the later weeks, most experimental subjects are above most control subjects. Individual lines vary a lot within each arm, so the group difference is clearest toward the end.

## Problem 3
```{r}
set.seed(1)

sim_t <- function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5, nsim = 5000) {
  map_dfr(1:nsim, \(i) {
    x <- rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
    broom::tidy(t.test(x, mu = 0)) |> select(estimate, p.value)
  }) |> mutate(mu = mu)
}

res <- map_dfr(0:6, sim_t)

summ <- res |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarize(power   = mean(p.value < 0.05),
            avg_all = mean(estimate),
            avg_rej = mean(estimate[p.value < 0.05]))

# Plot 1: power vs mu
ggplot(summ, aes(mu, power)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "True mu", y = "Proportion of null rejected (power)")

# Plot 2: average estimate, all vs rejected only
summ |>
  pivot_longer(c(avg_all, avg_rej), names_to = "which", values_to = "avg") |>
  mutate(which = recode(which, avg_all = "All samples",
                        avg_rej = "Only samples where null rejected")) |>
  ggplot(aes(mu, avg, color = which)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "True mu", y = "Average estimate of mu-hat", color = NULL)
```

Power increases with the true effect size $\mu$. Power is about 0.19 at $\mu = 1$, 0.57 at $\mu = 2$, 0.89 at $\mu = 3$, and 0.99 or higher for $\mu \geq 4$.

Across all samples, $\hat{\mu}$ is approximately equal to $\mu$, since the sample mean is unbiased. Among samples where the null was rejected, $\hat{\mu}$ is not equal to $\mu$ when power is low. When power is low, only samples with unusually large estimates reach $p < 0.05$, so the average of the rejected samples overestimates $\mu$. As power approaches 1, the two lines coincide.
